concept.name: Reverse stock split
concept.definition: A corporate action that consolidates shares - exchanging many old shares for one new share - to raise the per-share price proportionally while leaving market capitalization unchanged. It is most common among small or distressed companies trying to meet exchange minimum-price rules or attract institutional investors.
concept.intuition: It is the same pie cut into fewer, bigger slices: economically neutral by itself, but usually a symptom that the share price fell low enough to become a problem.
concept.mechanics: In a 1-for-N reverse split each holder receives one share per N owned and the price multiplies by N; fractional shares are typically cashed out. Exchanges enforce minimum bid prices, and FINRA processes OTC reverse splits as corporate actions after 10 days' advance notice, posting them to the OTC Daily List.
concept.formula: Post-split price = Pre-split price x N; Shares after = Shares before / N (for a 1-for-N split).
concept.failure_modes: Reverse splits often precede further decline because the underlying distress is untouched; they are strongly associated with low-priced, high-risk OTC names, and repeated reverse splits can trap holders in cascading dilution.
concept.misconceptions: A higher post-split price does not make the company more valuable or safer - FINRA stresses that a split does nothing to change the value of a company - and institutional interest rarely follows if the fundamentals do not improve.
concept.example: FINRA's illustration: 5,000 shares at $0.10 (a $500 position) become 25 shares at $20 in a 200-for-1 reverse split - the same $500 investment in fewer shares.
